rows.en: The books to which we allude are all the books written by Jews from this ancient period that are not included among our Holy Writings. The later sages gave them a special name and called them "outside books," and they forbade reading them. All these books were sealed with the seal of the opinions of their time, to a greater or lesser degree. Of the traces of beliefs and opinions that are in them we find many examples in all the books of the Oral Torah, and this shows that the spirit ruling in both the one and the other is the spirit of the ancient time. The book of Ben Sira was written some time after the death of Simeon the Just, and was translated into Greek by the author's grandson. The book of the Proverbs of Solomon was before the author's eyes. In countless places he uses the Proverbs of Solomon and expands them, and by his expansion we sometimes understand the sense of the proverbs that were before him. He also took as the basis of his inquiry ideas and figures of speech from the books of Psalms and Job. And whoever examines his words and proverbs with proper examination will find that the book of Ecclesiastes too was before his eyes; for it is no accident that in several chapters of his book (11:20–22; 14:3–17) he puts forward ideas whose like we find in Ecclesiastes, only Ben Sira expands them and puts them in more ornate language. But the expansion is a sign that in Ben Sira they are derivative and in Ecclesiastes they are primary, and not the reverse. And perhaps his words against inquiring into what is hidden, when he says: "Seek not what is too wonderful for you, and search not what is hidden from you," etc. (3:21), are aimed against all the doubts of Ecclesiastes. And when the author describes, at the end of his book, the excellence of King Solomon (47:14–20), he also mentions his songs, his figures of speech, his proverbs and his expositions. Now the words "songs, figures of speech, proverbs and expositions" we cannot understand unless we say that Ben Sira attributed three kinds of books to Solomon. And what are they? The Song of Songs, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes. From all this it appears that the foundations of the book were the opinions of the Torah, the Prophets and the other Holy Writings as they were understood in his time, and all in agreement with the opinions of the Pharisees. And therefore they copied the words of the book as though it were one of the Holy Writings, and according to the account of the Talmud, Simeon ben Shetaḥ already alluded to the words of Ben Sira. Indeed, in many places we find opinions and principles of religion in the mouths of the sages of the Torah whose exact like we find in Ben Sira, and this is a sign that those opinions and principles were the opinions of the ancient time. And it is fitting to list a few examples here in particular. Speaking of wisdom he says (1:1, 4) that it is from the Lord, and that it was before His works of old. And the source of wisdom is the Torah of the Lord (ibid. 5; 24:9, 25). And this is the opinion of the Pharisees at all times, that wisdom is the Torah (Mekhilta Beshallaḥ end of ch. 9, Ba-Ḥodesh ch. 10, and in many places, and in the Talmud and Midrashim). And he says that wisdom sought a dwelling place among all the nations, and at the Lord's command it dwelt among the people of Israel (44:6–9)⚠1; this agrees with the aggadah of our sages in the Talmuds, that all the nations were asked to accept the Torah (Avodah Zarah 2b; Mekhilta Ba-Ḥodesh ch. 5; and Sifre Deuteronomy pisqa 343). He who occupies himself with the Torah, said Ben Sira, is fit to stand guard over the affairs of state and religion, to instruct the people, to bring counsel to princes and to be appointed to every kind of office; and therefore such men shall not toil at labor and the work of the hands (38:23; 39:1–10). This agrees with the opinion of the sages of the Oral Torah: "Whoever takes upon himself the yoke of Torah, the yoke of government and the yoke of worldly occupation are removed from him." Against the ancient view that the sick man should trust in the Lord⚠2 and not consult a physician (II Chronicles 16:12), the sages laid down that the physician has been given leave by the Lord to heal, and said: "'And he shall surely heal' [Exodus 21:19]: this teaches that permission was given to the physician to heal" (Bava Kamma 85a). Ben Sira expanded this principle and decided that first of all one should entreat the Lord to send healing, and then entrust oneself into the hand of the physician, who is sent by the Lord to heal the diseases of the flesh (38:1–13). On divorcing a wife, too, he said: if his wife is not according to his wish, let him send her away, even if he has not found in her any unseemly thing (6:26; 25:29); this is according to the opinion of the Pharisees from the days of Simeon ben Shetaḥ and of the House of Hillel. And of a number of moral sayings in the Talmud the like is found in the book of Ben Sira, such as: "Repent one day before your death" (Shabbat 153a; Ben Sira 5:8); "Do not despise any thing" (Avot ch. 4; Ben Sira 5:18); "Be exceedingly lowly of spirit, for the end of man is the worm" (Avot ch. 2⚠3; Ben Sira 7:18); that one must not say to a penitent, "Remember your former deeds" (Sifra Qedoshim ch. 8; Bava Metzia 58b; Ben Sira 8:10); and many like these. From this we judge that his opinions are the opinions of the Pharisees in the Land of Israel at the time when he wrote. And now anyone who has a heart to understand will learn from this that many things in the Talmud and the Midrashim that are called by the name of one of their sages — which, as our eyes see it, we think are new, as though the one who said them brought them out of his own heart and devised them by the spirit of his understanding — are in truth old: the early ones already carried them on their lips generations before, those who came after them in the later generations preserved them, and their master⚠4 only collected them, to leave them as a blessing for the later generations. Besides the book of Ben Sira there are, among the outside books, writings that were composed in the Hebrew or Aramaic language and whose native land is the Land of Israel. The first is the First Book of the Hasmoneans [I Maccabees]. From its figures of speech it is recognizable that it was written in Hebrew; this book was already before the eyes of Josephus, and its writer was one of the Pharisees. The Book of Tobit too was written in Hebrew and in the Land of Israel. The writer's belief in the life of the world to come (2:18) and in angels and evil spirits, according to the opinions of the Pharisees, teaches us that he was one of the Pharisees. There are also allusions in it to statutes of the Oral Torah (6:24; 7:9; 10:16). The saying of Hillel, "What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow," is stated in it word for word (4:16). The Book of Baruch was written in Hebrew, and from beginning to end the spirit of the opinions of the Pharisees rules in it. We cannot decide clearly when it was written, but this is clear: the writer saw the book of Daniel and copied sayings from the prayer that is placed in Daniel's mouth (9:9–19); and whoever considers his words will find that he copied from Daniel and not the reverse{v1_11_13:1}; and he likewise copied a number of things from the book of Nehemiah. The Wisdom of Solomon, which the sages of Israel call "the great Wisdom of King Solomon," was attributed to King Solomon, and they thought that it was originally written in Hebrew by Solomon's own hand (Naḥmanides, introduction to the Torah; *Me'or Einayim*⚠5 ch. 57); and some Gentile scholars too held it to be the work of Solomon's hands. But in our time and in the generation before us the critics have agreed and concluded that its original is Greek, since it has distinct marks of Greek wisdom. Yet they admit that it differs from the other books that Jews in Alexandria composed on religion and the Torah, in that those made the secondary thing the main thing; but for this book Greek wisdom was not the main thing, but was like buds and flowers with which to adorn the wisdom of the Jews. And if it uses expressions taken from the writings of Greek philosophy, it does so only to make the matter sweet to Greek readers; and we already know that the sages of the Land of Israel did not refrain from accepting a number of things from Greek wisdom, to make them a spice for the Torah. The author of this book too did not refrain from using Greek opinions where they agree with the opinions of the Torah. Therefore, when we find in this book Greek figures of speech, or ideas and expressions whose content is usual in the books of the Greeks, this is no sign that its author stands in the position of the Jews in Alexandria; for the Jews in the Land of Israel too upheld and accepted a number of opinions and ideas from Greek wisdom. And he who says that its figures of speech in attributes and its abstract ideas are evidence that it followed the opinions of the Greeks and the philosophy of the Alexandrian Jews errs in two respects. First, the use of abstract attributes and ideas was not peculiar to the Greeks alone, for we already find it at times in the figures of speech of our Holy Writings, especially in the writings composed in the exile and after the return. And who would not be astonished to hear that the concept "everlasting light" could not have been current in the mouths of the Hebrews (Langen, *The Jews in Palestine* 28), when we see that it is already usual in the mouths of the prophets? And if the writer describes wisdom and says that it is a radiance of everlasting light, a pure mirror of God's working, and the image of His goodness (7:26), we shall not take from this a proof that the writer walked in the ways of the Alexandrian Jews (Langen, ibid.), since the writers of the Jews in the Land of Israel also walked in this way. In Ben Sira (17:7) we find: "the eye of God's wisdom, which He planted in the heart of man"; and he says (21:3): "the tooth of iniquity," and "the fear of God is the produce of wisdom"; and he says (34): "the visions of the night are images of vanity; as in water, face answers to face." Here we see before us that the use of abstract attributes was usual among the Jews of the Land of Israel. And second, we say: even if we admit that the author used Greek figures of speech, as befits anyone who writes in the Greek language, this is still no proof that the opinions of the book were not the opinions of the Jews in the Land of Israel. Indeed, whoever is versed in the words of our sages knows that all its opinions are hinted at, a little or much, in the words of the sages of the Land of Israel; and since the author described his opinions in Greek figures of speech, the opinions themselves became unrecognizable and were considered by many to be Greek opinions. But the truth is this (Langen, ibid. 34): this book is an offspring that came forth from the joining of the wisdom of the Jews with the wisdom of the Greeks; its flesh is flesh of the flesh of Jewish wisdom and bone of its bone, and Greek gave it its appearance and form. Therefore this book too is a book of remembrance that has preserved for us the opinions of the Jews in the Land of Israel in the time of the Temple. The Second Book of the Hasmoneans [II Maccabees], which is an abridgment of the book of the history of the Hasmonean war that Joshua [Jason] of Cyrene wrote in five books — although its source and birthplace is Alexandria, nevertheless, since its opinions are truly Jewish, it will be of use for our purpose.

1.note: Printed 44:6–9; the passage on wisdom seeking a dwelling and resting in Israel is Ben Sira 24:6–9 (probably כ"ד).

2.note: The print shows a letter like ד/ר with no clear mark; read as בד' (= in the Lord).

3.note: The saying מאד מאד הוי שפל רוח is in Avot ch. 4 (4:4), not ch. 2.

4.note: Printed ורוהם (or ורוחם), which gives no sense; read as ורבם, 'their master' (the sage named as author).

5.note: Expanded as Me'or Einayim (Azariah de Rossi), ch. 57, which discusses the Wisdom of Solomon; abbreviation not certain.

rows.en: Now we shall not pass on from here until we have said a few words about some books that were born among the Jews in the Land of Israel in this ancient period. They are: the Fourth Book of Ezra, the Book of Enoch, the Book of Jubilees. All three contain beliefs and opinions that grew on the soil of Israel, though as a whole they are "degenerate plants of a strange vine" [Jeremiah 2:21]. The Fourth Book of Ezra, by its spirit, is the work of a Jew of the Land of Israel. Whether it was written in Hebrew or in Greek, the opinions of the scholars are not in agreement, and to us it is all one in which language it was written. In the course of time many hands touched it for the benefit of other opinions. The book contains visions and prophecies attributed to Ezra. The content of the prophecies concerns the fate of the Israelite nation and the divine destiny appointed for it, the kingdom of the Messiah, the world of the resurrection, the last day of judgment, and the end of the kingdom of Rome. These matters are told in the book as a dialogue between Ezra and various angels. One prophecy contains a parable and its interpretation about the destruction of Rome by the Messiah, and alludes in it to twelve kings. But even with the interpretation it is like a hidden riddle. Many scholars of our time have sought to solve the riddle and did not succeed. But this is clear from the words of all of them: the book is not later than the destruction of the Temple{v1_11_14:1}. Opinions of aggadic midrash run all through the book, and in this respect it will be of use to us. Like it is the Book of Enoch, which contains visions and prophecies attributed to Enoch the righteous. Its purpose is to comfort his people in their toil. The content of the prophecies is like the prophecies of Ezra. It also speaks of the Nefilim and the sons of God who came in to the daughters of men, and it attributes to these angels, who corrupted their way, the invention of sorcery and of various arts; and it speaks of evil spirits and demons. The angels lead him to the ends of the earth and reveal to him the secrets of the heavenly and earthly world, and they show him a writing of God engraved on a tablet, of the deeds of men to the end of all generations. By the prophecies and announcements that he received from God and from the angels, he understands and beholds the history of man to the last generation, and he speaks of it in parable and image. He clothes the history of Israel and its troubles in the garment of parable. He divides the time of the world to its end into ten weeks, which include the history of the nation to the author's time; and there is no trace in it alluding to the time from the Hasmonean kingdom onward, apart from a few additions that are recognizable in it, which show traces of a somewhat later time. In the last two weeks he describes the kingdom of the Messiah, the resurrection and the last day of judgment, and he seals the book with general words of reproof and moral instruction. This is the main content of the book. Most of its critics thought that it was written scroll by scroll, and they also pointed out hints in it that its author was of the sect of the Essenes. And it is true that the course of his ideas is like the way of the Essenes. His inquiry into the secrets of the world and into the names of the angels and their workings — is this not also the practice of the Essenes? And special writings of this kind were already attributed to them (Jellinek, *Beit ha-Midrash* vol. 3, XXXII, note 4). But what has been pointed to as particular traces is not enough to decide. And if we find in the book that Enoch prayed at sunrise and praised the Lord who splits the windows of the firmament and brings the sun out of its place, to shine on the face of the heavens and run its course on high (ch. 82:12), this is no proof that the author was of the Essenes, who prayed before sunrise; for this is not a custom peculiar to the Essenes — did not the pious men of old (vatikin) among the Pharisees also do so? And the content of the prayer is like the content of our blessing of the Shema. They further point to his Essene character in that his mouth is full of the praise of the humble and of the reward appointed for them for their bodily self-mortification, and of the reward of those who are insulted by the wicked, who love the Lord and not silver and gold and the pleasures of the world, who accept sufferings and stand the test (in the last chapter), and several virtues like these (Ewald). But only one who knows the Pharisees and their customs from nothing but the writings of their opponents and slanderers will think so: he holds the Pharisees to be seekers of dominion, honor and pleasures, and the Essenes to be marked by the virtues of humility and patience. But whoever is versed in the words of the Pharisees and their teachings knows that these virtues are the foundations of Pharisaism; and the Essenes are marked by them not because they were Essenes and differed in their virtues from the Pharisees, but because they were of the Pharisees and held to the virtues of the Pharisees. Are not all these virtues found recorded and stated explicitly in the words of the Pharisees? They said: "By the merit of a man's humility he is delivered from Gehinnom" (Yevamot 102b). And who in their eyes was of those who truly love the Lord? "Those who are insulted and do not insult, who hear their disgrace and do not answer, who act out of love and rejoice in sufferings" (Shabbat 88b). And of whom did they say, "Happy are you in this world, and it shall be well with you in the world to come"? Of one who conducts himself by the virtue of contentment: "who eats bread with salt, drinks water by measure, sleeps on the ground, lives a life of hardship and toils in the Torah" (Avot ch. 6). And now, is not the content of these words exactly the content of what is written in the Book of Enoch? However that may be, it is clear that this book contains the opinions of the Jews in the time of the Temple, and in this respect it is fitting for us to pay attention to it in this place. Likewise it is fitting to pay attention to the Book of Jubilees, which is called Bereshit Zuta. Its character is that of an aggadic midrash. Many aggadot found in our aggadic midrashim have found their place in it (Jellinek, ibid. XII). Several words of the book are explained by our midrashim (Beer, in *The Relation of the Book of Jubilees to the Midrashim* 25). In the manner of the masters of aggadah it gives reasons for the commandments of the Torah, and in its interpretations it follows the way of the masters of midrash. Who was the author, and what was his name? It has not been made known to us. But it is clear that he lived and wrote his book in the Land of Israel, and that he was one of the masters of aggadah, for at all times there were "rabbis of aggadah." Sometimes his words are against the halakhah, but this is no proof that he was of the sect of those who opposed the teaching of the Pharisees. Do not the masters of aggadah in general sometimes expound the verses not in accordance with the halakhic midrash, though they were of the Pharisees? And if one of the masters of aggadah says, by way of example, that one who has intercourse with a Gentile woman transgresses "You shall not sow your field with two kinds," "You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together," and "You shall not wear mingled stuff" (Yalkut Deuteronomy, remez 931), which contradicts the halakhah, we shall not say on this account that the expounder is not among the sages who follow the halakhah. And moreover, who will give us the measure of which of the halakhot was in practice in the days of the writer of this book, so that we could know that if he denied some halakhah found among us, this is a sign that he is opposed to the Pharisees, the masters of the halakhah? Indeed, just as one cannot judge from his agreement with the opinion of the Pharisees in some of his words and say that he was a Pharisee out of love for their teaching, so one cannot judge the reverse from his contradictions{v1_11_15:1}. It is not part of our purpose to describe the history of the book here; we shall only remark that there is nothing in it indicating that the author was an Alexandrian (Frankel) or that he was a Dositheian of the sect of the Kutim [Samaritans] in Alexandria (Beer). Rather, the language of the book from beginning to end shows that it was written in Hebrew, and the spirit that rules in it is the spirit of the aggadah of Jerusalem; like all the sons of his land he glories in Jerusalem and in the Sanctuary on the site of Mount Zion (ch. 1), and in most of his words he agrees with the Pharisees on matters of the commandments and is strict about the performance of the commandments; and all this is a sign that he was neither an Alexandrian nor a Kuti. But this too is plain to see: the author meant to cast doubt on the Pharisees concerning their custom of intercalating the years and sanctifying the month by sighting; with harsh words he challenges the intercalators of the years and says of them that they corrupt the times, the months, the Sabbaths and the festivals (ch. 6). Yet this is not the way in which the Kutim and the Boethusians challenged it, who sought to mislead Israel; rather his challenge is directed against their reckoning, in that they reckoned by the days of the moon and sanctified the month by sighting in agreement with their reckoning, whereas in his opinion the years should be reckoned by the days of the sun. And who will tell us that there were not among the Pharisees themselves individuals who did not approve of the practice of the court in sanctifying the month and intercalating the year, when we see that some of the greatest of the Tannaim cast doubt on the court's reckoning and were grieved that they sanctified the month on the word of witnesses whose testimony was contradicted by their reckoning? And from such a challenge to a challenge against the reckoning by the days of the moon is only a short step. In sum, one cannot pass judgment on the author and say that he did not follow the Pharisees because he sometimes departs from their midrash, just as we do not say so of Josephus, who also sometimes departed from the midrash of the Pharisees; and Josephus himself testifies of himself that he is of the Pharisees. And indeed it is so, that the general principles of religion hinted at in this book are founded on opinions and beliefs that were alive in the people in his time. Like these three books, other outside books were born in the Land of Israel in that time, and from all of them there is profit for one who inquires into the antiquities of the nation, its opinions and its beliefs.

footnotes.en: Herzfeld, vol. 1, 318, is in doubt as to who copied from whom; but it seems to me that in the Book of Baruch it is a copy. Right at the beginning of the prayer (1:15) it uses the saying "To You, O Lord, belongs righteousness, and to us shame of face" (Daniel 9:7); it abridged Daniel's prayer and omitted some of the sayings in verse 7. And from verse 8 it took the saying "also to the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem, to our kings and our princes, to the priests and to the prophets," and expanded and changed the wording. In verse 16 Baruch speaks with the Lord in the second person, and at once in verse 17 in the third person: "and we did not hearken to His voice, to keep His commandments and His statutes that He commanded us." This is because he kept the wording of the verse in Daniel (9:10), and did not take care that in Daniel the third-person speech is right, since Daniel began in verse 9 to speak in the third person; but the author of the Book of Baruch omitted verse 9, and therefore it is strange that he spoke in the third person in verse 17. This is only because he kept the wording that he copied. In chapter 2:17 he says, in the wording of Daniel (9:18), "Incline Your ear and hear, open Your eyes and see." In Daniel the words "open and see" fit, being directed at "our desolations and the city"; but the author of the book completes the saying with the verse from Psalms, "for in death there is no remembrance of You" [Psalms 6:6], and for this the words "open and see" are strange and forced. Therefore it seems that it is only a copy.

On the composition of this book see *Die jüdische Apokalyptik* by Dr. Hilgenfeld, and *The Opinions of the Jews in the Land of Israel at the Time of the Renewal of the Christian Religion* [*Das Judenthum in Palästina zur Zeit Christi*] by Dr. Langen.

On the history of this book: Jellinek, in his introduction to *Beit ha-Midrash*, vol. 3; Treuenfels, in the journal *Orient*, 1846; Beer, in *The Relation of Jubilees to the Midrashim*; Frankel, in his journal, 1856; Dillmann, in Ewald's yearbook, vols. 2 and 3; Langen, in *The Opinions of the Jews in the Land of Israel at the Time of the Founder of the Christian Religion*. And in the journal *Ha-Shaḥar*, year 1, published by Mr. Peretz Smolenskin, there is a Hebrew translation by Dr. Solomon Rubin with an introduction that covers the history of the book, and he proves with clear proofs that it was composed in the Hebrew language.
